title: Waterfall — Network Request Timeline Simulator
description: A millisecond-step simulator of a fictional storefront loading thirteen requests across four origins, drawn as an animated waterfall with queue, DNS, TCP, TLS, TTFB and download phases plus a main-thread lane. Switch between approximate network profiles, flip HTTP/2, compression, preload, defer, async and lazy-loading, and watch the critical request chain, the FCP and LCP markers and the per-type byte budgets react.
prompt: Build 'Waterfall', a network request timeline simulator for a fictional page. Give it a realistic set of resources — HTML, CSS, JS, a web font, images and an API call — with sizes, priorities and dependencies, spread across a few origins. Let me pick a network profile (fast 4G, slow 4G, 3G, clearly labelled as approximate) and toggle HTTP/2 multiplexing, preload, defer, async, lazy-loading and compression. Actually simulate it: shared bandwidth, connection setup per origin, the six-connection limit on HTTP/1.1, parser-blocking scripts, discovery through CSS. Render an animated waterfall with DNS / connect / TLS / TTFB / download segments, highlight the critical request chain, and mark FCP and LCP. Add per-type budgets that turn red when exceeded. Make it look like an instrument panel, not a dashboard template.

methodology: Model-level oracles: byte totals are hand-checked sums of the resource table (161 KB of compressed JS, 512 KB raw, 426 KB of images) so budget maths is asserted exactly, not approximately.

Metamorphic relations for the timing model: a slower profile must never make FCP or LCP earlier; preload must move the hero's start before the end of the HTML and improve LCP; defer must cut FCP when a script is the render blocker.
Causal checks on the critical chain: with compression off on slow 4G the chain is html → vendor.js, and deferring vendor.js removes it from the chain and flips its main-thread execution to 'defer'.
Protocol behaviour: HTTP/2 uses one connection per origin (4 total); HTTP/1.1 opens more and several same-origin requests show their own TCP + TLS segments.
Persistence and budgets: editing a budget turns the row green immediately and survives a reload.
Responsive and wider-font review at 1280, 390 and 360 px: the waterfall keeps a fixed label column and percentage-positioned bars so it never scrolls sideways.
risks: Circular dependencies in the model (font discovery depends on first styling, which depends on scripts sharing the same bandwidth) — solved by re-evaluating gates every simulated millisecond.
Tuning resource sizes can silently flip which resource limits LCP, breaking chain expectations.
Animated clip-path reveal could hide bars from a screenshot or a test taken mid-animation.
qa.playwright: Everything the spec needs is written onto the DOM as data attributes — each row's start, end, segment list and critical flag, each metric's milliseconds, each budget's used value and over state — so no assertion depends on bar pixel widths. The simulation is deterministic (a fixed 1 ms step, no randomness), so exact values like the 512.0 KB JS total are safe to assert while timings are compared relationally. emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' }) skips the 1.8 s reveal animation, which removes any need for waits or page.clock. Visual screenshots were reviewed by hand rather than committed with toHaveScreenshot, because font rendering differs across machines.
coverage: Network profile switching, radio state and approximate labelling
Compression off: exact JS and image totals, JS budget over, bytes increase
Budget edit clears the warning and persists across reload
Render-blocking vendor.js on the critical chain, then deferred off it; async tag.js
Preload moves hero and font starts earlier and improves LCP; request detail panel
HTTP/1.1 extra connections and handshakes; lazy-load skips four requests

a11y: Network profiles are an arrow-key radiogroup, toggles are aria-pressed buttons, and every waterfall row is a button with a spoken summary (type, size, priority, start and end, critical status) that opens a text breakdown in a live region. Metric changes are announced politely, and budgets show text status alongside the colour.
